c.tagline: One of the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities, rebuilding around its ancient citadel and souqs.

taxi.fareNote: Meters are rarely used; agree the fare with the driver before departing or have your hotel arrange the ride. Shared microbuses (servees) running fixed routes are the cheapest option. Fares are paid in cash, and US dollars are often accepted or preferred alongside Syrian pounds.

emergency.note: 112 reaches police and 110 the ambulance service; dispatchers may not speak English, so ask hotel staff to help. Emergency infrastructure is still being rebuilt after the war.

avoid.reason: Avoid the heavily damaged former front-line districts of eastern Aleppo, where rubble and unexploded ordnance remain, and stay away from military installations; most governments advise against all travel to Syria.
Expect frequent checkpoints, never photograph soldiers or government buildings, and stay on well-trodden paths because of unexploded ordnance.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed walled old town, dominated by the great medieval Citadel of Aleppo and threaded with the covered lanes of Al-Madina Souq, the Great Umayyad Mosque, khans, and hammams; much is undergoing post-war reconstruction, but restored courtyard houses now serve as boutique hotels. Best for travelers who want to be inside Aleppo's ancient core.

The historic Christian quarter just north of the old city, a warren of narrow alleys, ornate courtyard mansions, churches, and Syrian-Ottoman facades, now home to some of the city's atmospheric boutique hotels, cafes, and restaurants; suits travelers wanting heritage character and evening dining.
A leafy central district of early-20th-century buildings, including the storied Baron Hotel, plus mid-range hotels, shops, and restaurants; a practical, relatively lively base close to the old city.
The modern downtown around Bab al-Faraj, Saadallah al-Jabri Square, and the main hotels, banks, and transport links; convenient and central, though busier and less atmospheric than the old quarters.

The newer residential and university districts spreading west, with wider streets, apartment blocks, larger hotels, and everyday services; quieter and more spread out, suited to longer or business-oriented stays.

water.note: War-damaged infrastructure makes supply intermittent; drink bottled water only.

transit.pay: Fares are paid in cash directly to the driver or conductor; there is no smart card or app-based ticketing. Fares are very low, and US dollars are commonly used alongside Syrian pounds.
transit.hours: Buses and microbuses run roughly 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM; taxis fill in for later travel.
transit.note: Aleppo has no metro or tram; the city relies on state buses and shared microbuses (servees) on fixed routes, supplemented heavily by taxis, as services continue to be rebuilt after the war.

train: Aleppo (Baghdad) Railway Station - long-distance passenger rail is largely suspended and being restored after war damage
bus: Aleppo main bus/microbus stations with intercity coaches to Damascus, Hama, Homs, and Latakia

airport.name: Aleppo International Airport (ALP)
rentals: Local agencies at the arrivals hall (major international chains are not currently operating)

transit.m: Taxi to the city center (20-25 min) — the most reliable option; agree the fare before departing
Microbus/servees toward central Aleppo where available

tip.r: Rounding up and leaving around 5-10% at restaurants is customary; small tips to drivers, porters, and guides are appreciated. Cash only, and small US-dollar notes are welcome.
